section_summary: This section assesses Japan’s capacity to finance rising military expenditure, focusing on government bonds, bank holdings, prices, wages, foreign exchange, and the balance of payments. It includes State Department analysis and comments, embassy reports on Finance Minister Yuki’s policies, and reports of spending for the North China conflict. The final pages begin a detailed compilation of Japan’s 1937–1938 budget and its supporting documents.

people.name: H. H. Kung
people.role: Participant in a discussion of Japanese finances in Paris

people.name: Eugene H. Dooman
people.role: Counselor of the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo

people.name: Senjuro Hayashi
people.role: Japanese prime minister and minister for education

people.role: Japanese minister for agriculture and forestry

people.role: Japanese minister for commerce and industry and minister for railways

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese public finances, concluding pages
subfiles.about: The memorandum weighs Japan’s ability to finance military spending against bond-market, labor, and foreign-payments pressures.
subfiles.summary: Banks may absorb further government bonds, though tighter credit, inflation fears, and stagnant wages threaten domestic financing. Trade deficits, spending in Manchuria, and depleted exchange reserves create stronger external pressure. The analysis anticipates increasing economic controls if spending continues.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the Financial and Economic Annual of Japan for 1936
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy sends three copies of Japan’s 1936 financial and economic annual.
subfiles.summary: Transmits three copies received from the Japanese government.

subfiles.title: Comments on the memorandum concerning Japan’s public finances
subfiles.about: The division proposes revisions and a more explicit conclusion for the economic adviser’s study.
subfiles.summary: The comments address credit for the earlier study, wages and export competitiveness, Manchukuo’s possible contribution to army costs, and taxation. They urge a conclusion that recognizes both Japan’s capacity to keep financing military spending and the political and social strains it imposes.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum for the revised study of Japan’s finances
subfiles.about: The economic adviser submits an updated study and proposes sending it to the president.
subfiles.summary: Submits the revised study and recommends forwarding a copy to the White House.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Concerning the Financial and Economic Aspects of the Japanese Situation
subfiles.about: The study reappraises Japan’s ability to sustain military spending and its mounting external-payment problems.
subfiles.summary: The study documents rising budgets, deficits, debt, and government bond holdings, concluding that banks can probably finance further spending, though they may face pressure to do so. Its tables track bank assets, debt service, prices, wages, exchange rates, trade, capital movements, and gold. It identifies the adverse balance of payments and military outlays in Manchuria as major vulnerabilities, and examines exchange controls and gold exports as limited remedies. Public acceptance of sacrifice and labor unrest remain political uncertainties.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting the financial and economic memorandum
subfiles.about: The department sends the embassy three copies of its confidential April 20 study.
subfiles.summary: Encloses three copies for the embassy’s information.

subfiles.title: Finance Minister’s Speech of April 20
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports Finance Minister Yuki’s address to bankers on budgets, production, imports, and investment.
subfiles.summary: Yuki links defense spending to higher production and urges selective import control, private investment in Manchuria and China, and bank financing aligned with national policy. Grew notes a stock-market decline after the speech and broadly favorable press comment.

subfiles.title: Broad Economic Control Inevitable, States Yuki in Address to Bankers
subfiles.about: A newspaper account presents Yuki’s economic and financial policy speech.
subfiles.summary: The article reports Yuki’s case for greater productive capacity, selective import controls, foreign trade, and access to raw materials. It also describes his positions on currency stability, bank lending, investment in Manchukuo and China, and budget planning that accounts for commodity supplies.

subfiles.title: File note on Bank of Japan gold shipments
subfiles.about: A cross-reference points to a telegram about gold shipments to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Notes three shipments, with later lots intended to support yen exchange operations.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese finances discussed in Paris
subfiles.about: A cross-reference points to a conversation between Kung and Ambassador Bullitt.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to a telegram on their discussion of Japan’s finances.

subfiles.title: Telegram on prospects for drastic financial control
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: The embassy reports concern that military spending may force drastic financial controls.
subfiles.summary: Reports Domei’s account and suggests the government may be assigning responsibility to the military.

subfiles.title: Partial paraphrase of Tokyo telegram No. 158
subfiles.about: A paraphrase conveys the embassy’s report on possible financial controls.
subfiles.summary: Repeats concerns about a managed economy and the embassy’s interpretation of the press report.

subfiles.title: Transmission of paraphrase to the Treasury
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards copies of the Tokyo telegram paraphrase.
subfiles.summary: Encloses six copies of the paraphrase of telegram No. 158.

subfiles.title: Financial and Economic Memorandum
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy acknowledges receipt of the April 20 study.
subfiles.summary: Says the embassy is studying the memorandum and will send comments.

subfiles.title: Office of Naval Intelligence forwarding note
subfiles.about: A largely illegible handwritten note appears to forward an attached item on Japanese financial policy.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten forwarding note; most of its text is illegible.

subfiles.title: Fundamental Financial Policy of Hayashi Cabinet Outlined by Finance Minister Yuki
subfiles.about: A press report summarizes cabinet approval of Yuki’s financial policy.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes policy on armaments, production, debt, interest rates, exchange, trade, gold shipments, and living costs.

subfiles.title: File note on North China incident appropriation
subfiles.about: A cross-reference identifies a telegram on new spending for the North China incident.
subfiles.summary: Notes Diet approval of ¥96.8 million in addition to an earlier cabinet allotment.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Peiping, Tientsin, and North China spending
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy reports Japanese statements on the fighting and a new North China appropriation.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Office spokesman Kawai describes possible autonomy movements in the Peiping–Tientsin area and assigns blame for fighting to Chinese forces. The Diet has approved ¥96.8 million for the North China incident, with further spending expected.

subfiles.title: Japanese Budget, April 1, 1937 to March 31, 1938
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy explains Japan’s 1937–1938 budget and the borrowing behind its appropriations.
subfiles.summary: The despatch distinguishes the general, supplementary, extra, and special-account budgets and estimates borrowing authorized across them at roughly ¥965 million. It identifies military appropriations, Manchurian expenses, reserves, and subsidies dispersed through different accounts. Dooman cautions that the accounting structure obscures the full cost of Japan’s program in China.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance Relating to the Budget Estimate for Fiscal Year 1937–38
subfiles.about: The ordinance promulgates the approved budget and sets fiscal rules for continuing expenditure and borrowing.
subfiles.summary: Sets revenue and expenditure at ¥2,813,937,971 and permits up to ¥500 million in Treasury notes and borrowing.

subfiles.title: Budget for Fiscal Year 1937–1938: general budget compilation
subfiles.from: Japanese government; compiled by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The enclosure presents the general budget’s summary figures and begins its detailed revenue and expenditure tables.
subfiles.summary: The compilation compares the amended Yuki budget with the earlier Baba proposal and prior-year figures. It itemizes ordinary and extraordinary revenues, including ¥770.8 million in loans and contributions from Manchukuo and special accounts. Page 160 begins the departmental expenditure detail; the budget enclosure continues beyond this section.
